uncited: It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Ray Marching with Reflections](1963-ray-marching-with-reflections.md) by operating entirely within the 2D screen coordinate system and utilizing the existing depth buffer, rather than marching through a 3D volume or scene graph.
This makes it significantly cheaper than full ray tracing but limited to visible geometry.
*   Shaded point position in world space ($P_{world}$).
*   View vector ($V$) from the camera to $P_{world}$.
*   Depth buffer (Z-buffer) containing depth values for all visible pixels.
*   Color buffer (G-Buffer or Final Color Buffer) containing radiance/color values for all visible pixels.
*   Reflected color contribution ($C_{refl}$) for the shaded point.
*   **Depth Buffer:** A 2D array of size $W \times H$, storing depth values ($z$) typically in clip space or view space.
*   **Color Buffer:** A 2D array of size $W \times H$, storing RGB(A) color values.
**Reflect View Vector:** Calculate the reflection direction $R$ by reflecting the view vector $V$ along the surface normal $N$.
**Initialize Ray:** Start a ray at $P_{world}$ with direction $R$.
**Iterate Ray Steps:** Advance the ray in screen space.
Compute the current world position $P_i$ of the ray.
Project $P_i$ into screen space to get pixel coordinates $(u_i, v_i)$.
Fetch the depth value $z_{buffer}$ from the Depth Buffer at $(u_i, v_i)$.
Fetch the depth value $z_{ray}$ of the current ray point $P_i$ in the same coordinate system as the depth buffer.
*   If $z_{ray} > z_{buffer}$ (assuming depth increases away from camera), the ray has passed behind the geometry in the depth buffer.
This indicates an intersection occurred between the previous step and the current step.
*   If $z_{ray} < z_{buffer}$, the ray is in front of the geometry; continue to the next step.
*   If the ray goes off-screen or exceeds a maximum distance, terminate.
**Binary Search Refinement:** If an intersection is detected between step $i-1$ and step $i$, perform a binary search between these two positions to find a more precise intersection point $P_{hit}$.
**Sample Color:** Once $P_{hit}$ is determined, project it to screen space $(u_{hit}, v_{hit})$.
Sample the Color Buffer at $(u_{hit}, v_{hit})$ to obtain the incident radiance $C_{refl}$.
**Shade:** Combine $C_{refl}$ with the base shading of the surface.
Geometry outside the viewport is not reflected.
*   **Time Complexity:** Linear with respect to the number of ray steps and pixels processed.
Each pixel requires a depth buffer lookup and potentially a binary search.
*   **Memory Complexity:** $O(W \times H)$ for the depth and color buffers.
*   **When to use:** Real-time rendering of reflections and color bleeding where full ray tracing is too expensive.
*   **When not to use:** When reflections of off-screen objects are required, or for non-Lambertian surfaces if the source constraint is strict.
